source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF (Addiction, doi:10.1111/add.14486), 21 PDF pages, all read (pdftotext -layout); every number used checked on rendered pages at 150 dpi: PDF pp. 2, 6, 9, 10, 11, 19 (Table 1) and 20 (Table 2). Pages cited as PDF p. N (no journal pagination in this version).

claims.overstatement: None for the Victorian part. Small omissions: (1) 8 of the 243 model deaths were misadventure deaths from heroin intoxication, while the national count as selected here took only poisoning (or F11/F19) underlying causes with T40.1, so a few of the 78 lie outside the national definition by design rather than being misrecorded; (2) the 20 deaths with no code at all were put down by the authors to late initial registration (never assessed by the ABS), not to wording, so the claim could say why; (3) 'the coroner attributed' follows the paper's own definition, which counts heroin named either in the cause of death or in the NCIS 'object that caused death' field; (4) the authors' own limitation, that the ABS revision process changed after 2013 (associated-cause toxicity codes are now revised), is not mentioned and bears on whether the gap persists.
claims.note: Every Victorian number in the statement and magnitude was found and recomputed: 243 (180 with 6-AM, so 63 without, editors' arithmetic correct); 161 of 243 coded T40.1, 82 not (33.7%, so 34% correct); 4 coded deaths excluded as coincidental; 161 + 4 = 165 and 243 - 165 = 78; 191 heroin-attributed (180 + 11), 154 coded (146 + 8), 37 not; 34 of 39 morphine or other opioid and 5 of 5 generic not coded; 5 of the 44 non-heroin-attributed deaths coded T40.1; 20 with no code. Reporting issue relevant to 'mostly because of the wording': the abstract's split of the 82 missed deaths (40% morphine or non-specific certification, 30% heroin-attributed with irregular certification, 24% late registration) cannot be rebuilt from Table 2, which gives 39 of 82 (48%) and 37 of 82 (45%); it only fits if the 20 uncoded deaths were first taken out of the attribution groups, which implies that roughly a dozen of the 37 heroin-attributed missed deaths were late registrations rather than wording failures (my inference; no cross-tabulation is printed). 'Mostly' still holds; the paper's 'vast majority' is less certain. The model is the same group's earlier one (ref. 30, Stam et al., 2017), called 'gold standard' by the authors and not validated in this paper; no intervals are given.

anchors.locator: Results > The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Broad NCIS search returned 9,060 cases; the authors' model identified 243 heroin-related deaths in Victoria, 2012-2013, 180 of them with 6-AM detected; 235 were heroin toxicity deaths and 8 misadventure deaths from heroin intoxication. AIHW data held 165 deaths assigned T40.1 (associated cause) by ABS coders, all 165 found among the NCIS search results; 78 fewer than the model count.

anchors.locator: Results > Discrepancies in the assigned classification and coding > Comparison of the cases assigned the heroin-specific ICD-10 code of T40.1 (paragraph continuing onto PDF p. 10)
anchors.extracted: Of the 243 model deaths, 161 carried T40.1 and 82 did not, so were not counted as heroin deaths in AIHW/ABS data. Four further deaths coded T40.1 were excluded by the model because heroin use was judged coincidental rather than a direct contributor to death (161 + 4 = 165).

anchors.locator: Results > Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st paragraph; Table 2
anchors.extracted: Heroin toxicity attribution 180, 146 coded T40.1 (81%); heroin and morphine 11, 8 (73%); together 191, 154 coded (81%), 37 not. Morphine or other opioid attribution 39, 5 coded (13%); generic drug toxicity 5, 0 coded; the 44 deaths not attributed to heroin included 5 (11%) coded T40.1. Misadventure 8, 2 (25%). Total 243, 161 coded (66%).

anchors.locator: Results > Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 2nd paragraph and bullet list
anchors.extracted: Of 37 heroin-attributed toxicity deaths without T40.1, 3 named heroin in the cause of death but were coded T40.2 only (a coding error); most of the rest were missed through how the cause was written: a generic cause ('mixed' or 'combined drug toxicity') with the drugs only in the Object field; morphine in the cause-of-death field with heroin only as an object; or a complication such as hypoxic brain injury written first.

anchors.locator: Results > Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
anchors.extracted: By underlying cause, X44 (other and unspecified drugs) held the largest gap: 98 model deaths against 69 AIHW deaths (29). Twenty model deaths had another underlying-cause code and 20 had no ICD-10 code at all; case closure took a median 15.5 months (IQR 6, range 10-30), so the authors put the 20 down to delayed initial registration, after which the ABS never coded them, not to slow investigations.

Of the missed deaths, 40% came from attribution to morphine toxicity or non-specific drug-toxicity certification, 30% from heroin-attributed deaths with irregular certification, and 24% from late initial registration with the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages; heroin deaths were underreported by 32% (78 of 243). These shares cannot be rebuilt from Table 2 (39 of 82 and 37 of 82) without a cross-tabulation the paper does not print.

anchors.locator: Methods > Heroin-related deaths and study period, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Methods > Heroin-related deaths identified through the NCIS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Heroin converts rapidly to 6-AM and then morphine, so morphine may reflect heroin or morphine itself; after a long interval (including resuscitation and hospital admission) 6-AM may be undetectable, and 6-AM is unstable, hydrolyses in post-mortem samples and keeps poorly frozen (cited literature). Cases were closed NCIS files (usually autopsy and toxicology report, police narrative, coronial finding), assessed with the group's earlier model weighing toxicology (6-AM, morphine-to-codeine ratio or morphine alone) with investigative evidence, and used as the 'gold standard'.

anchors.locator: Methods > Heroin-related deaths from the AIHW and ABS, bullet list; Methods > Identified causes of variation, 1st paragraph (last sentence)
anchors.extracted: The national count took deaths registered in Victoria, occurring in 2012-2013, open or closed, with T40.1 as an associated cause and an underlying cause of X42/X44, X62/X64, X85, Y12/Y14 (or F11/F19 before 2013). A death counted as 'attributed to heroin' when heroin appeared, alone or with other drugs, in cause of death lines 1a-3 or as a primary or secondary 'object that caused death'.

The authors caution against extending the findings to later data: after 2012-2013 the ABS revision process changed so that associated-cause toxicity codes, not only the underlying cause, are revised when more information arrives.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: Table 2 gives 39 and 37 of the 82 missed deaths (48%, 45%), not 40% and 30%.
165 = 161 + 4, so Table 1's AIHW column holds the 4 excluded deaths and its row differences are net.
Seen on the rendered PDF p. 2.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI-prevalence, overall moderate, is reasonable. Domain 1 could also record that the reference includes 8 misadventure deaths, while the comparison count was restricted to poisoning (or F11/F19) underlying causes, so the two counts are not defined alike.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the Methods label the model as the authors' own 'gold standard'. The Discussion's 'actual number' wording and its unquantified claim of morphine over-reporting are the main overreach, and the card lists both.

missed: Definitional mismatch (PDF pp. 7, 9; Table 1, PDF p. 19): the national count took T40.1 only with a poisoning (X42/X44, X62/X64, X85, Y12/Y14) or F11/F19 underlying cause, so the 8 misadventure deaths in the reference could enter it only if coded as poisonings. Part of the 78-death net gap is therefore definitional rather than misrecording. They probably sit among the 20 deaths with another underlying-cause code, but this is not cross-tabulated.

The 20 uncoded deaths probably overlap the 37 heroin-attributed missed deaths. If the abstract's 30% (about 25 of 82) is right, roughly 12 of the 37 were never coded (late registration) rather than missed through wording, so the paper's 'vast majority' through wording (PDF p. 11) is not shown in numbers. This is an editors' inference; it bears on how firmly key finding 6 and any claim can say 'mostly because of the wording'.
